To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we provide a novel framework for quantifying the control performance level as the transmission interval changes, and we provide stability results for the class of UGES protocols, which include RR and TOD protocols.

we have developed new techniques to quantify the performance of nonlinear delayed networked control systems as the transmission interval changes and to provide the maximal allowable transmission interval for which the desired performance level is attained.

we provide a methodology for quantifying the robustness of networked control systems with respect to networked phenomena and that we show that the robustness is improved by using model-based estimators.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: how to stabilize a nonlinear system with delayed dynamics using a networked controller, and for given plant-controller dynamics, how to quantify the control performance as the transmission interval is varied?
the design of a networked control system that is capable of stabilizing a given plant in the face of network-induced disturbances and delays.
the design of nonlinear controllers and scheduling policies for networked control systems with the objective of stabilizing the closed-loop system in the presence of network-induced phenomena.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our results provide a systematic and unified framework to analyze the robustness of nonlinear networked control systems with respect to network induced phenomena and to determine the maximal allowable transmission interval for a given networked system.
our approach is able to stabilize nonlinear networked systems with delays and disturbances for a wider class of communication networks and scheduling protocols.
we have provided a methodology that can be applied to a wide range of nonlinear systems with time delays, and that can handle a wide range of scheduling protocols.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the present results are the first to quantify the control performance of nonlinear delayed networked control systems (NDCSs) in the presence of network-induced phenomena and UGES protocols.
the proposed methodology can be applied to nonlinear systems and can provide stability results for a larger set of scheduling protocols than the ones considered in the literature so far.
we provide a systematic methodology to study the robustness of nonlinear delayed networked control systems with respect to networked phenomena.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the proposed stability results can be employed to quantify the robustness of the closed-loop system with a given network-induced phenomenon and to design the communication network to ensure a prespecified level of control performance.
the proposed methodology allows for MATI-based design of networked control systems with nonlinear dynamics and variable delays.
the MATI is a useful tool to characterize the performance level for a given plant-controller dynamics, network-induced phenomena, and scheduling protocol.
